info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 9.2: Automated Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Gazetteer Lookup.

name.text: 01 Question: From Hand Craft to Automated Processing: Scaling Entity Recognition

questiontext.text: Why do digital scholars transition from manual entity annotation to automated Natural Language Processing (NER) pipelines?

generalfeedback.text: Automated NER scales entity identification across large textual corpora that would be impractical to annotate entirely by hand.

answer.text: Manual markup is precise but too slow to scale across large archival corpora containing thousands of manuscript pages.

feedback.text: Correct. While manual annotation establishes rigorous gold standards, automated tools are required to analyze extensive archival corpora at scale.

answer.text: Manual markup is forbidden by international copyright laws once a document exceeds one hundred words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Copyright law does not prohibit manual scholarly transcription or markup.

answer.text: Automated tools eliminate 100% of errors and never require human verification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automated models regularly make errors on historical texts, necessitating careful auditing.

answer.text: Computers refuse to display XML files that were typed by human beings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers process valid XML regardless of how it was created.

name.text: 02 Question: How Computers Read Names: Statistical Sequence Models

questiontext.text: How do statistical sequence models like SpaCy identify named entities in running text?

generalfeedback.text: Statistical sequence models use contextual weights trained on large corpora to predict entity tags probabilistically.

answer.text: They evaluate tokens and their surrounding contexts using probabilistic machine learning weights trained on annotated language corpora.

feedback.text: Correct. Modern sequence models use contextual embeddings and statistical transition weights to predict entity spans and types.

answer.text: They connect directly to the human author's mind using telepathic sensors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Statistical NLP models rely on mathematical probability and training corpora, not telepathy.

answer.text: They consult a hard-coded alphabetical list containing every word in existence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Static lists are gazetteers; statistical models predict entities based on probabilistic context.

answer.text: They randomly assign entity tags using a digital coin toss.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models optimize predictions mathematically based on contextual training features.

name.text: 03 Question: The IOB2 Tagging Standard: Inside, Outside, Beginning

questiontext.text: In the IOB2 tagging scheme, what does the 'B-' prefix indicate?

generalfeedback.text: The IOB2 standard uses B- (Beginning), I- (Inside), and O (Outside) to delimit entity boundaries cleanly.

answer.text: The beginning token of a multi-token or single-token named entity span.

feedback.text: Correct. 'B-' marks the initial token of an entity, distinguishing it from subsequent 'I-' (inside) tokens or 'O' (outside) tokens.

answer.text: A binary token that represents computer bytecode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In IOB2 notation, 'B' stands for 'Beginning'.

answer.text: A bad or corrupted token that must be deleted from memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'B-' is a standard structural label marking the start of an entity span.

answer.text: A background color applied to web browser typography.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IOB2 is a token annotation format, not a CSS display rule.

name.text: 04 Question: Two Main Tools: SpaCy and Rule-Based Gazetteers

questiontext.text: What is the difference between a statistical NER tagger (like SpaCy) and a rule-based gazetteer?

generalfeedback.text: Gazetteers match known names deterministically; statistical models predict entities contextually.

answer.text: SpaCy generalizes based on sentence context and patterns, while a gazetteer matches exact pre-compiled lists of known names.

feedback.text: Correct. Gazetteers look up known strings deterministically, whereas statistical models infer entities probabilistically from surrounding context.

answer.text: SpaCy works only on numbers, while gazetteers work only on punctuation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both tools process natural language words.

answer.text: Gazetteers are neural networks running in the cloud, while SpaCy is a printed dictionary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SpaCy is a Python NLP library, and gazetteers are structured lookup lists.

answer.text: There is no difference; SpaCy and gazetteer are synonyms for the exact same algorithm.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They represent fundamentally different paradigms: deterministic lookup vs. probabilistic sequence modeling.

name.text: 05 Question: A 10-Line Python NER Pipeline in VS Code

questiontext.text: In a standard SpaCy Python script, what object is created when text is passed through the loaded language pipeline (`doc = nlp(text)`)?

generalfeedback.text: Passing text into a SpaCy pipeline generates an annotated Doc object containing processed tokens and entity spans.

answer.text: A Doc container object holding processed Token and Span objects with linguistic and entity annotations.

feedback.text: Correct. Calling nlp(text) runs the pipeline and returns a Doc object containing tokens, sentences, and entity spans (doc.ents).

answer.text: A compressed audio recording of the manuscript being read aloud.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SpaCy produces structured linguistic data structures, not audio files.

answer.text: A blank text document with all letters replaced by zeros.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Doc preserves tokens, text, and rich morphological attributes.

answer.text: A raster graphic image of the original manuscript page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. SpaCy operates on textual strings and tokens, not raster images.

name.text: 06 Question: SpaCy Entity Labels: PERSON, GPE, LOC, and ORG

questiontext.text: In standard SpaCy pipelines, what does the entity label 'GPE' represent?

generalfeedback.text: GPE (Geopolitical Entity) identifies administrative units like nations and cities, distinguishing them from physical landmarks (LOC).

answer.text: Geopolitical Entity: countries, cities, and states with defined governments.

feedback.text: Correct. GPE designates political territories (cities, nations), distinct from non-political geographic landmarks (LOC).

answer.text: General Purpose Equipment: tools, machinery, and furniture.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GPE stands for Geopolitical Entity.

answer.text: Grammatical Prepositional Element: conjunctions and adverbs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GPE is a named entity label, not a part-of-speech category.

answer.text: Global Positioning Error: distorted satellite navigation data.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GPE is a semantic entity category used in information extraction.

name.text: 07 Question: The Out-of-Vocabulary Problem: Historical Orthography Traps

questiontext.text: Why do modern pre-trained models like `en_core_web_sm` frequently fail on early modern documents?

generalfeedback.text: Domain mismatch and historical orthography cause out-of-vocabulary failures in models trained on modern corpora.

answer.text: They are trained on modern news and web text, making them struggle with archaic spellings, capitalization habits, and obsolete syntax.

feedback.text: Correct. The Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) problem arises because training data distributions diverge sharply from historical manuscript orthography.

answer.text: Because early modern documents contain dangerous computer viruses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts are harmless human linguistic records.

answer.text: Because pre-trained models refuse to process text written in the Roman alphabet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. English and French models process Roman alphabets natively.

answer.text: Because eighteenth-century scribes deliberately scrambled their letters to trick future computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical scribes wrote according to the standard conventions of their own era.

name.text: 08 Question: Boundary Errors: Where Does a Name Begin and End?

questiontext.text: What is a classic boundary error in automated entity extraction?

generalfeedback.text: Boundary errors clip titles, drop name components, or absorb adjacent punctuation into the entity span.

answer.text: Tagging 'Governor Hopson' as only 'Hopson', omitting the title or capturing trailing punctuation.

feedback.text: Correct. Boundary errors occur when a model clips a vital part of a name or absorbs adjacent non-entity words.

answer.text: Changing the font color from black to purple in the terminal window.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Terminal styling has nothing to do with entity token boundary extraction.

answer.text: Converting an English word into an ancient Greek translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Boundary errors concern span coordinates, not linguistic translation.

answer.text: Saving a text file with an illegal filename extension.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File naming is an operating system task separate from token span detection.

name.text: 09 Question: Entity Type Confusion: Mixing Up Places, Groups, and People

questiontext.text: Which example illustrates entity type confusion in an automated NER model?

generalfeedback.text: Entity type confusion occurs when an algorithm correctly locates a name but assigns it to the wrong semantic class.

answer.text: Classifying 'Assemblée nationale' as a PERSON rather than an ORG.

feedback.text: Correct. Type confusion occurs when the span boundaries are correct but the assigned semantic category is wrong.

answer.text: Recognizing 'Paris' as a place located in France.

feedback.text: Correctly identifying Paris as a place is accurate classification, not confusion.

answer.text: Failing to find the word 'and' in a sentence.

feedback.text: Conjunctions are not named entities, so omitting them is correct behavior.

answer.text: Printing the text to a desktop printer without paper.

feedback.text: Printer hardware errors are unrelated to entity type confusion.

name.text: 10 Question: Cohort Corpus A Tests: Ace and the 1791 French Decree

questiontext.text: When Ace runs `fr_core_news_sm` on the 1791 French Revolutionary decree, which language feature challenges the model?

generalfeedback.text: French historical contractions (l', d') and institutional titles challenge default modern tokenization and tagging.

answer.text: Elided determiners and prepositions like 'l'Assemblée' and 'd'Orléans', which modern tokenizers may fail to split cleanly.

feedback.text: Correct. French contractions and historical royal/legislative formulas test the limits of modern news-trained tokenizers.

answer.text: The entire text being written in Chinese pictograms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree is written in eighteenth-century French.

answer.text: The manuscript containing only numerical accounting tables without words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree is a legislative narrative text.

answer.text: The French language having no nouns or adjectives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French possesses rich morphological and nominal structures.

name.text: 11 Question: Cohort Corpus B Tests: Olyvia and Maud Lewis's Letters

questiontext.text: Why does `en_core_web_sm` struggle to detect entities in Olyvia's Maud Lewis correspondence?

generalfeedback.text: Informal personal letters lack the formal journalistic context that standard statistical models expect.

answer.text: Informal colloquial mentions like 'Everett' lack institutional titles or formal journalistic sentence context.

feedback.text: Correct. Intimate epistolary style diverges from the formal journalistic prose used to train standard news models.

answer.text: Maud Lewis wrote her letters entirely in mathematical equations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud Lewis wrote informal personal English letters.

answer.text: The letters were typed on a digital word processor with spellcheck enabled.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The letters were hand-painted or handwritten on paper.

answer.text: Personal letters are legally exempt from Natural Language Processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Any textual document can be analyzed using NLP tools.

name.text: 12 Question: Cohort Corpus C Tests: Andromeda and the 1752 Treaty

questiontext.text: In Andromeda's 1752 Treaty, what causes automated models to misclassify 'Major Jean-Baptiste Cope'?

generalfeedback.text: Complex historical titles and intercultural naming conventions frequently mislead automated statistical classifiers.

answer.text: The military title 'Major' combined with hyphenated French forenames in an eighteenth-century English diplomatic treaty.

feedback.text: Correct. Cross-cultural naming conventions and military honorifics confuse single-language modern models.

answer.text: The treaty was written in computer machine binary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The treaty is written in eighteenth-century diplomatic English.

answer.text: The text contains no names of any human beings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The treaty prominently names Mi'kmaw and British signatories.

answer.text: Treaties are always rejected by Python libraries as invalid syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python processes treaty text without difficulty.

name.text: 13 Question: Measuring Machine Accuracy: Precision, Recall, and F1-Score

questiontext.text: What does the Recall metric measure in named entity evaluation?

generalfeedback.text: Recall measures completeness: what percentage of all real ground-truth entities did the model capture?

answer.text: The proportion of true entities from the human ground truth that the automated model successfully found.

feedback.text: Correct. Recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives), measuring coverage completeness.

answer.text: The physical speed at which the computer processor completes the calculation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Processing speed is execution throughput, not recall accuracy.

answer.text: The percentage of predicted entities that turned out to be correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is the definition of Precision, not Recall.

answer.text: The number of spelling errors found in the original manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recall measures model retrieval performance, not scribal errors.

name.text: 14 Question: Understanding Error Types: False Positives vs. False Negatives

questiontext.text: What constitutes a False Positive in named entity recognition?

generalfeedback.text: A False Positive is an incorrect detection: the model claimed something was an entity when the ground truth says it is not.

answer.text: The model predicts an entity where none exists in the ground truth, or tags a common noun as a name.

feedback.text: Correct. A False Positive is an erroneous prediction, incorrectly claiming a non-entity or wrong span as a name.

answer.text: The model correctly identifies a person and assigns the correct name.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a True Positive.

answer.text: The model completely misses a real historical person mentioned in the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Missing a real entity is a False Negative.

answer.text: The model turns off the computer monitor during execution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hardware states are not classification error types.

name.text: 15 Question: Automated Gazetteers: Matching Names Against Pre-Compiled Lists

questiontext.text: What is the primary strength and primary weakness of a pure gazetteer lookup approach?

generalfeedback.text: Gazetteers provide rock-solid precision for known entries, but fail completely on novel or uncatalogued variants.

answer.text: It achieves 100% precision for known names on its list, but has zero recall for novel names or variant spellings not included.

feedback.text: Correct. Gazetteers cannot recognize uncatalogued variants (poor recall), but match listed names reliably (high precision).

answer.text: It runs infinitely fast but destroys all files on the hard drive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Gazetteers are safe string-matching algorithms.

answer.text: It can read handwritten manuscripts from photos without OCR, but cannot read print.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Gazetteers operate strictly on digital text strings.

answer.text: It requires quantum computing hardware to run simple searches.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Gazetteers are simple, lightweight dictionary lookups.

name.text: 16 Question: SpaCy EntityRuler: Combining Rules with Statistical Models

questiontext.text: How does the SpaCy `EntityRuler` enhance a statistical NER pipeline?

generalfeedback.text: The EntityRuler blends rule-based patterns and gazetteers directly into SpaCy's pipeline to correct statistical blind spots.

answer.text: It injects deterministic pattern-matching rules and gazetteer lists directly into the pipeline, overriding or supplementing statistical predictions.

feedback.text: Correct. The EntityRuler combines rule-based precision with statistical breadth, allowing custom rules to patch known model weaknesses.

answer.text: It physically measures the margins of the manuscript page in inches.

feedback.text: Incorrect. EntityRuler is a software component for pattern matching, not a physical measuring stick.

answer.text: It translates the entire text into Latin before parsing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. EntityRuler matches token patterns in the target language.

answer.text: It deletes all statistical machine learning models from the computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. EntityRuler works harmoniously alongside statistical taggers.

name.text: 17 Question: Exporting Automated NER to TEI XML: Building ner_baseline.xml

questiontext.text: Why must automated NER predictions be exported into valid TEI XML before running a comparative benchmark?

generalfeedback.text: Exporting predictions to TEI XML aligns machine outputs with the manual baseline for direct scientific auditing.

answer.text: To allow direct, automated token-by-token comparison against the manual ground-truth XML baseline.

feedback.text: Correct. Structuring both manual and automated predictions in matching TEI format enables systematic diffing and scoring.

answer.text: Because Python scripts cannot write data to any format other than TEI XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python can output JSON, CSV, plain text, and many other formats.

answer.text: Because Moodle crashes if non-XML files exist in the project directory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Moodle does not inspect internal local development files.

answer.text: Because historical manuscripts cannot be stored in modern databases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts are regularly stored across many database architectures.

name.text: 18 Question: The VS Code Side-by-Side Diff Audit

questiontext.text: How does an editor perform a side-by-side diff audit between `ground_truth_entities_manual.xml` and `ner_baseline.xml` in VS Code?

generalfeedback.text: VS Code's side-by-side diff view enables rapid, visual auditing of disagreements between manual and machine markup.

answer.text: By selecting both files in the file explorer and choosing 'Compare Selected' to visually highlight every tag and boundary disagreement.

feedback.text: Correct. VS Code's diff viewer highlights additions, deletions, and structural divergences side-by-side in color.

answer.text: By printing both files onto transparent plastic sheets and holding them up to a window.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code provides built-in digital diff capabilities on screen.

answer.text: By deleting both files and rewriting them from memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Auditing requires comparing the existing files directly.

answer.text: By running an audio converter to listen to the files simultaneously.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual diffing is visual and programmatic, not acoustic.

name.text: 19 Question: Building the Discrepancy Table in NER_BENCHMARK.md

questiontext.text: What information should be recorded for each entry in the `NER_BENCHMARK.md` discrepancy table?

generalfeedback.text: The discrepancy table documents token spans, expected tags, machine predictions, error categories, and philological causes.

answer.text: Token span, manual ground truth tag, machine prediction tag, error classification, and philological explanation.

feedback.text: Correct. A thorough discrepancy audit logs what was expected, what was predicted, the error type, and the root cause.

answer.text: The weather outside the library and the temperature of the room.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Environmental weather is irrelevant to computational text benchmarking.

answer.text: The price of the student's laptop computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hardware costs do not belong in a textual discrepancy report.

answer.text: The names of all students enrolled in other university departments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The discrepancy table focuses on the text under investigation.

name.text: 20 Question: Preprocessing with Module 6 Normalization

questiontext.text: How does applying Module 6 orthographic normalization before running NER improve automated performance?

generalfeedback.text: Orthographic normalization reduces out-of-vocabulary errors, allowing modern models to recognize historical name tokens.

answer.text: Standardizing historical spelling variants (e.g. historical 's', contractions) brings words closer to the modern training vocabulary of the model.

feedback.text: Correct. Normalizing archaic typography resolves out-of-vocabulary mismatches, significantly increasing recall.

answer.text: It deletes all consonants from the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting consonants renders the text unreadable.

answer.text: It changes the historical text into modern slang.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly normalization standardizes historical orthography without rewriting semantics.

answer.text: It replaces all proper names with generic numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Entity recognition requires preserving name tokens.

name.text: 21 Question: Token Alignment and Overlapping Spans

questiontext.text: What problem occurs when an automated tagger splits a hyphenated word that the manual baseline treated as a single token?

generalfeedback.text: Token alignment must be preserved or reconciled to calculate accurate mathematical precision and recall scores.

answer.text: Token misalignment, making automated 1-to-1 evaluation impossible without alignment mapping.

feedback.text: Correct. Discrepant token boundaries break automated evaluation matrices unless an alignment map reconciles character offsets.

answer.text: The hard drive immediately formats itself.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Software token mismatch does not damage hardware.

answer.text: The text automatically translates into French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenization differences do not trigger language translation.

answer.text: The computer operating system cancels the student's enrollment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Academic enrollment is handled by university administrative servers.

name.text: 22 Question: Entity Linking: From Tagged Spans to External Records

questiontext.text: What is the distinction between Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Named Entity Linking (NEL)?

generalfeedback.text: NER identifies entity boundaries and types; NEL resolves those entities to unique authority records (e.g. Wikidata Q-numbers).

answer.text: NER detects name spans and categories in text; NEL resolves those spans to specific external authority database records.

feedback.text: Correct. Recognition finds the mentions (who/where), while linking connects them to canonical database identifiers (which exact person/place).

answer.text: NER is for books, while NEL is for newspapers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both techniques apply across all genres of text.

answer.text: NER is done by humans, while NEL can only be done by hand with a pencil.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both tasks can be executed manually or automated programmatically.

answer.text: There is no distinction; NER and NEL are identical synonyms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recognition and linking are two distinct phases of the information extraction pipeline.

name.text: 23 Question: Wikidata API Queries in Python

questiontext.text: How does a Python script query the Wikidata API to find potential matches for an entity string?

generalfeedback.text: Python queries the Wikidata `wbsearchentities` API to retrieve candidate Q-identifiers and descriptions automatically.

answer.text: By sending an HTTP GET request to the `wbsearchentities` action endpoint with the search string and language parameters.

feedback.text: Correct. The MediaWiki API endpoint `wbsearchentities` returns structured JSON candidate records with descriptions and Q-identifiers.

answer.text: By sending a printed postcard to the Wikimedia Foundation headquarters in California.

feedback.text: Incorrect. APIs provide instantaneous automated programmatic access over HTTP.

answer.text: By scraping every web page on Wikipedia into a local text file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scraping the entire encyclopedia is inefficient; the API provides targeted querying.

answer.text: By executing a shell command that shuts down the local network router.

feedback.text: Incorrect. API queries use standard network communication.

name.text: 24 Question: The Ambiguity Trap in Automated Linking

questiontext.text: Why must automated entity linking results be carefully verified when searching for common names?

generalfeedback.text: Automated search often defaults to prominent modern figures, requiring human disambiguation for historical entities.

answer.text: Multiple historical figures often share identical names, and automated scripts may link to the most famous modern person instead of the historical actor.

feedback.text: Correct. Popularity-ranked API results frequently return modern celebrities rather than eighteenth-century colonial or revolutionary figures.

answer.text: Because Wikidata deliberately gives false answers to test students.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikidata is a collaborative open knowledge base, not a deceptive test.

answer.text: Because the internet cannot transfer historical data across national borders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Internet protocols transmit all digital text globally.

answer.text: Because search algorithms only return results written in German.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikidata supports multilingual querying across dozens of languages.

name.text: 25 Question: Handling Verified Absences in Automated Pipelines

questiontext.text: What should an automated linking pipeline do when an API search returns zero matching records for a historical person?

generalfeedback.text: Automated pipelines must flag zero-match queries as Verified Absences and mint local identifiers rather than confabulating links.

answer.text: Assign a local project identifier, flag the entity as a Verified Absence, and log it for human review.

feedback.text: Correct. Graceful handling records the absence and assigns a local identifier rather than crashing or assigning a false match.

answer.text: Invent a random 8-digit number and pretend it is a real Wikidata Q-ID.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inventing fake identifiers corrupts linked open data integrity.

answer.text: Crash the entire pipeline and delete all previously parsed documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pipelines should catch missing records and log them gracefully.

answer.text: Replace the person's name in the document with 'Unknown'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial pipelines never alter the primary historical text.

questiontext.text: What is the primary role of the `NER_BENCHMARK.md` report in your project repository?

generalfeedback.text: NER_BENCHMARK.md documents experimental precision, recall, F1 scores, and error analyses for reproducible research.

answer.text: To formally record experimental methodology, performance metrics (P/R/F1), error taxonomy breakdowns, and curated discrepancy tables.

feedback.text: Correct. The benchmark document provides a transparent, reproducible scientific audit of automated tool performance.

answer.text: To serve as a marketing advertisement to sell the software to commercial companies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NER_BENCHMARK.md is an open scholarly research report.

answer.text: To complain about the difficulty of university examinations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Academic reports maintain professional scholarly focus.

answer.text: To provide a fictional narrative about time travel.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The report documents empirical computational linguistics experiments.

name.text: 27 Question: The Error Taxonomy: Four Reasons Machines Fail

questiontext.text: What are the four categories in our course error taxonomy for automated NER?

generalfeedback.text: Our error taxonomy diagnoses failures across OOV orthography, boundary errors, type confusion, and contextual ambiguity.

answer.text: Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) Orthography, Boundary Errors, Entity Type Confusion, and Contextual Ambiguity / Polysemy.

feedback.text: Correct. Our course taxonomy classifies errors into OOV orthography, boundary slips, type confusion, and contextual ambiguity.

answer.text: Hardware Overheating, Low Battery, Bad Monitor, and Broken Mouse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are hardware maintenance issues, not linguistic error classes.

answer.text: Syntax Errors, Indentation Errors, Memory Errors, and Type Errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are generic Python programming runtime errors.

answer.text: Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner, and Dessert.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are daily meals, not computational error categories.

questiontext.text: How can an editor demonstrate pipeline improvement in `NER_BENCHMARK.md`?

generalfeedback.text: Iterative pipeline refinement demonstrates how targeted rules improve recall and overall F1 performance.
